title: KOSPI Close November 9, 2026: Falls 0.81% to 5,018.85, KOSDAQ -0.82%
content:
KOSPI closed at 5,018.85, down 0.81%, and KOSDAQ closed at 638.97, down 0.82%, after both indexes rose more than 2% early on dip buying and a rebound in U.S. chip stocks, then gave back those gains. Individual themes still moved: a control contest at Hanjin KAL, information security, chip back-end and test equipment, and optical cable names.

1. Rebound attempt fades — dip buying after last week's plunge

KOSPI opened at 5,034.20 (-0.51%) and rose as high as 5,172.94 (+2.24%) as dip buying came in after last week's sharp fall. KOSDAQ also reached 658.66 (+2.23%). Both gave back the gains in the afternoon and closed slightly lower.

A rebound in U.S. chip stocks on Friday helped sentiment: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 4.21%, with AMD and Micron among the strong names, drawing bounce buying into Korean chip stocks. Samsung Electronics (+0.64%) and SK hynix (+0.35%) rose. Institutions, mainly financial investment firms, led the buying.

On KOSPI, foreign investors net sold about 690 billion won and individuals about 490 billion won, while institutions net bought about 720 billion won.

2. Hanjin KAL control contest — airline and preferred shares surge

The share contest between Hoban Group and Hanjin Group Chairman Cho Won-tae drew attention. Hoban's side is reported to hold 20.69% against 20.58% for Cho's side, raising the chance of a fight for control. Markets also watched further stake purchases and a possible voting contest at a future shareholders' meeting.

Hanjin KAL preferred hit the daily upper limit, as did Korean Air preferred and Asiana IDT. The strength in preferred shares reflects hopes tied to the dispute and their relatively small float.

3. Information security — financial sector security spending

Buying spread across information security stocks on news of higher security investment in the financial sector. Cyberattacks and personal data leaks aimed at financial firms have kept drawing attention, and regulators are pushing integrated security monitoring, tighter control of outside access and sharing of hacking threat information. Hansak hit the upper limit and other security names rose with it.

4. Semiconductors — back-end, test equipment and PCB names

Chip stocks that had been under pressure rebounded. Expectations rose again for capital spending tied to the AI chip market and for demand for high-performance chip testing and back-end processing. Demand for high-performance memory and packaging used in AI servers and data centers drew attention across test equipment, inspection equipment and PCB makers.

5. Mercury returns to profit — optical cable and telecom infrastructure

Mercury hit the upper limit after reporting a third-quarter operating profit of 4.0 billion won, a swing from a loss a year earlier. Sales rose 29.1% to 38.2 billion won, and growth in optical cable supply drove the improvement. As AI data center investment grows, high-capacity optical links between servers matter more, and hopes for 5G upgrades and next-generation 6G networks lifted telecom equipment stocks. RFHIC rose more than 17% at one point and closed up 14.11%.

Quick FAQ

How did KOSPI and KOSDAQ close on Nov 9?
KOSPI closed at 5,018.85 (-0.81%) and KOSDAQ at 638.97 (-0.82%). Both rose more than 2% early before giving back the gains.

Why did Hanjin KAL stocks surge?
Hoban Group's side reportedly holds 20.69% against 20.58% for Chairman Cho Won-tae's side, raising the chance of a control contest, and preferred shares with a small float drew heavy buying.

Why did security stocks rise?
Repeated cyberattacks and data leaks at financial firms, plus regulators' push for stronger security monitoring, raised hopes for more security spending.
